idiom_name: Arc<[u8]>/Bytes handles in-process, an object-store key across processes
implementation_notes: Rust gives the cheap-reference half of the pattern for free - Arc<T> and bytes::Bytes clone in O(1) by bumping a reference count, so passing a payload inside one process is already a claim check without a store - which leaves the external store as the real work: aws-sdk-s3 (or an object_store crate) writes the payload, preferably streamed with ByteStream::from_path so it never has to sit in the message or in the heap twice, and the object key is what travels. Ownership doubles as the lifecycle policy: a Drop guard can delete the object exactly once, and a weak reference expresses a claim check that must not keep the payload alive. Use the external form whenever the message crosses a process or host boundary; inside one process, cloning an Arc is already reference passing and adding a store would only add a hop.
pitfalls: Bytes and Arc share memory only inside one process; a serialised message copies the payload anyway, so the claim check pays off only when the data is written once to a real store.

Retries make deletion dangerous: deleting the object after a partial failure can drop a payload another consumer still needs, so deletion must be tied to an explicit claim-once protocol rather than to the first successful read.
Blocking the async runtime with std::fs or a synchronous SDK call inside a tokio task stalls unrelated tasks - use the async APIs or spawn_blocking for local spooling.
